chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Type III usually leads to ambulation loss in adolescence, but the impact of disease-modifying therapies on this outcome has not been systematically studied. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Disease-modifying therapies halve the risk of ambulation loss and extend walking ability by more than a decade, with the greatest benefit in type IIIA. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These results support early and widespread treatment to preserve ambulation and provide new benchmarks for care, counselling and trial design. Introduction Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetically determined neuromuscular disorder that impacts motor neurons and their associated motor units, leading to muscle atrophy and weakness. The primary cause of the SMA phenotype is related to mutations in the survival motor neuron ( SMN1 ) gene situated on chromosome 5q13. Individuals with the mildest SMA type, type III or IV, acquire the ability to walk independently. Type III is further subclassified into type IIIA, with symptom onset before age 3, and type IIIB, with onset after age 3. Motor function is progressively compromised even in type III, with persistent weakness, leading to gait impairments, fatigue and, in many cases, eventual loss of ambulation (LOA). In a recent review synthesised natural history data from 22 arms across 7 studies, the median time to LOA in the overall population was estimated to be 13.4 years, encompassing a total population of 1327 individuals with type III. Further stratification based on SMA subtype revealed that for type IIIA, the median time to LOA was 13.4 years, while for type IIIB, it extended significantly to 44.2 years. Nonetheless, the 25th percentiles for the risk of LOA varied substantially—from 7.0 to 25.0 years—across different pooling scenarios, highlighting the heterogeneity within the type III population. The therapeutic landscape of SMA has been transformed by the advent of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), which target the underlying genetic deficiency of the SMN protein. Currently approved DMTs—including nusinersen, onasemnogene abeparvovec and risdiplam —increase SMN protein levels through different mechanisms and have shown significant clinical benefit, particularly when initiated early in the disease course. Several studies have reported the beneficial effects of the available drugs using functional scales, but a critical gap remains in understanding the extent to which these therapies influence the timing or likelihood of losing ambulation in comparison with the well-known natural history of LOA in type III. Given that maintaining ambulation is a major functional priority, understanding the impact of treatment on this outcome is critical for both clinical management and individual counselling regarding the expectations for individuals living with type III. This study aims to address this gap by evaluating the risk of LOA in individuals with type III undergoing DMTs. Methods This study is a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from the International Spinal Muscular Atrophy Consortium registry, which includes centres from Italy, the UK and the USA. Within this framework, data were systematically gathered prospectively through a structured electronic case report form (eCRF). Data were extracted from the registry from January 2025 to April 2025. Participants were eligible for inclusion if they had a confirmed diagnosis of type III, known age of symptom onset and known SMN2 copy number. Individuals of any age and any sex assigned at birth were considered. Participants receiving DMTs were included only if they were being treated with approved therapies, in the countries where this study was conducted, both nusinersen and risdiplam are approved to be used commercially for type III. Follow-up data from individuals who initiated investigational products were censored at the time investigational treatment began. Individuals who received DMTs prior to symptom onset were also excluded. LOA was defined as the inability to walk 10 m unassisted. Statistical analysis Data are presented as median and IQR for continuous variables and as frequency and percentage for categorical variables. To compare characteristics between included and excluded individuals, a χ²/Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical variables, while the Mann-Whitney U test was applied for continuous variables. Age at LOA was calculated from the date of birth to the date of the event. For those who remained ambulatory, follow-up was censored at the date of last contact. The association between DMT initiation and LOA was estimated using time-dependent Cox proportional hazards models. In these models, DMTs were included as a time-dependent covariate: individuals were assigned a value of 0 before DMT initiation and 1 after treatment began. This approach was necessary to avoid immortal time bias—that is, the period during which individuals must survive to receive treatment, which would otherwise be incorrectly attributed to the treatment group and artificially inflate its apparent benefit. By modelling treatment as time-dependent, individuals contributed person-time to the untreated group until the actual start of treatment, serving as appropriate controls for those receiving treatment during the same period.

By modelling treatment as time-dependent, individuals contributed person-time to the untreated group until the actual start of treatment, serving as appropriate controls for those receiving treatment during the same period. The following covariates were considered and selected a priori: age at symptom onset, sex, SMN2 copy number, year of birth and country. The year of birth was included to account for calendar bias, as access to diagnosis, standards of care and treatment availability have evolved over time and may influence outcomes independently of treatment. Adjustment for age at symptom onset further helps control for differences in disease severity and timing of clinical presentation—even among individuals born in the same year—ensuring a more accurate comparison of treatment effects across individuals with different disease trajectories. Statistical tests were conducted using R (V.4.3.2) and SAS (V.9.4; SAS Institute). A p≤0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results The initial cohort included 655 individuals with type III, 388 classified as type IIIA and 265 as type IIIB ( ). Their median age at last follow-up was 28.76 (22.9 in IIIA and 36.1 in IIIB) years. Of the 655 individuals, 218 (33%) lost ambulation (156 with type IIIA and 62 with type IIIB). Among the 156 IIIA, 148 (95%) lost ambulation before DMT initiation (n=144, 97%) or within 1 year after starting DMTs (n=4, 3%). Among the 62 IIIB, 54 (87%) lost ambulation before DMT initiation (n=53, 98%) or within 1 year after starting DMT (n=1, 2%). Among the 304 IIIA and IIIB individuals who had been on DMTs for more than 1 year, 283 (93%) remained ambulatory. presents details on age at first DMTs as well as the time from DMTs to LOA or last follow-up categorised by SMA subtypes IIIA and IIIB and ambulatory status. shows the percentage of individuals losing or not losing ambulation subdivided by treatment status (treated vs not treated) at event and by age groups at LOA or last follow-up. shows individual details of ambulatory status according to age at DMT initiation and DMT duration at event. Survival analysis Of the 655 individuals with type III eligible for survival analysis, SMN2 copy number was not available in 100 individuals, resulting in a final sample of 555 individuals (84.7%). Baseline characteristics of individuals included and excluded from the analysis are shown in . 503 of the 555 individuals (90.6%) started DMTs at a median age of 17.41 years (IQR 9.49, 33.00), while 52 (9.4%) individuals did not receive any DMTs. No significant differences were found between individuals who received and those who did not receive DMTs during the follow-up and individuals who never received DMTs in terms of sex, age at diagnosis, age at symptoms onset, year of birth and copy number. Of the 503 who received DMTs, 105 were on risdiplam-only, 333 were on nusinersen-only and 65 switched from nusinersen to risdiplam. presents the demographic characteristics of treated-population and never treated groups. The median age at LOA in all type III was 32 years in untreated periods and 44 years during DMTs ( ). Exposure to DMTs was significantly associated with a reduced risk of ambulation loss (HR=0.50; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.80; p=0.004). Older age at symptom onset was associated with a lower risk of ambulation loss (HR=0.82 per year; 95% CI 0.78 to 0.85; p<0.0001). The risk of LOA was more than twice as high in males, indicating that females had a significantly lower hazard (HR=2.05; 95% CI 1.56 to 2.70; p<0.0001). Individuals with four or more SMN2 copies had a significantly lower risk compared with those with two copies (HR=0.29; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.48; p<0.0001), while no significant difference was observed in individuals with three copies (HR=0.82; 95% CI 0.51 to 1.30; p=0.391). Among the 105 individuals treated with risdiplam-only, 2 (2%) lost ambulation during treatment. Of the 333 treated with nusinersen-only, 16 (4.8%) lost ambulation during treatment. Among the 65 who received both DMTs, 3 (4.6%) lost ambulation during DMTs (all occurred while on nusinersen, the first DMTs received). Due to the small number of events, along with notable differences in group sizes and baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, formal statistical comparisons were not performed, as they would likely lack sufficient power and could be misleading. Future studies specifically designed to capture DMT effects, including through the use of exclusively treated cohorts, would be necessary to facilitate a meaningful comparative analysis. Discussion Several studies have reported LOA in type III individuals. Zerres et al reported that the risk of losing ambulation increased over time in individuals with type III. Specifically, in type IIIA, the probabilities of remaining ambulatory at 10, 20 and 40 years after disease onset were 73%, 44% and 34%, respectively. In contrast, individuals with type IIIB had a more favourable prognosis, with 97%, 89% and 67% still ambulatory at the same time points. As confirmed by a recent meta-analysis, LOA is still a frequent finding even in more recent natural history studies performed before the advent of the DMTs with a median age of LOA of 13.4 years for IIIA and 44.2 years for IIIB. The full extent to which DMTs may change LOA has not been well defined as yet. While the short-term efficacy of the new DMTs on motor function has been reported by several studies, few studies have concentrated on LOA as this requires a longer period of observation. As DMTs have been available for nearly a decade, it is now possible to start analysing the data obtained in children and adults with type III to explore the possible effect of the DMTs on LOA. Interestingly, across our whole cohort of type III individuals, the percentage of treated individuals who lost ambulation was very low. This held true for the great majority of type III individuals, including those with type IIIA reaching puberty, who in natural history had a much higher risk of losing ambulation. It should be noted that in the small group of 21 treated individuals who lost ambulation, 5 lost ambulation within a year from starting DMTs. All individuals in this subgroup, even if able to walk more than 10 m independently, were only able to perform very limited distances on the 6 min walk test or were unable to complete it for safety reasons, these findings suggesting the need for early treatment. In order to better quantify the possible effect of DMTs on LOA, we performed a time-dependent analysis. As most individuals in our cohort transitioned from being untreated to receiving DMTs during follow-up, a time-dependent Cox regression model was chosen to account for immortal time bias. This approach was essential to avoid overestimating treatment effects by properly accounting for the time individuals spent untreated before starting therapy. The analysis provided strong evidence of the effectiveness of DMTs in reducing the risk of LOA among individuals with type III. In the overall type III cohort, exposure to DMTs was associated with a 50% reduction in the hazard of LOA (HR=0.50; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.80; p=0.004), when compared with untreated individuals. This demonstrates a substantial therapeutic benefit when administered during the ambulatory phase. In addition to DMTs, other key prognostic factors were identified. This demonstrates a substantial therapeutic benefit when administered during the ambulatory phase. In addition to DMTs, other key prognostic factors were identified. Males and individuals with 2 SMN2 copies had a significantly higher risk of LOA compared with females and individuals with four copies. Prior studies have documented more severe phenotypes in affected males compared with female siblings, and sex-specific differences in ambulatory ratios among SMA type III patients. Several mechanisms may contribute to this sex difference, including potential neuroprotective effects of oestrogen, sex-specific differences in SMN protein regulation, or differential expression of modifier genes on sex chromosomes. There were no significant differences in risk of LOA adjusting by country or year of birth, suggesting that variations in standards of care across countries and potential calendar bias did not significantly affect the risk of LOA in this cohort. The significantly reduced risk of LOA with later age at symptom onset (18% lower risk of LOA per additional year) (HR=0.82; 95% CI 0.78 to 0.85; p<0.0001) likely suggested a possible difference between IIIA (onset before 3 years) and IIIB (onset after 3 years). This was confirmed by the subgroup analyses revealing a significant interaction emerging between DMTs and type III subtype (p=0.029). The change in median age at ambulation loss in the whole type III cohort, increasing from 32 years in untreated individuals to 44 years in treated individuals, was mainly driven by the III A subgroup who showed a much lower risk of LOA (66%). In type IIIA, the median age at LOA changed from 14 years in untreated to 39.6 years in treated individuals, suggesting that the exposure to DMTs was strongly protective in this subgroup (HR=0.34; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.64). In contrast, the effect of exposure to DMTs was not significant in type IIIB (HR=0.93; 95% CI 0.42 to 2.06). This likely reflects the potentially slower progression of this subtype in which LOA does not always occur or, when this happens, may occur very late in life. Although males and individuals with fewer SMN2 copies (2 SMN2 vs 4+ SMN2 ) had a higher baseline risk of LOA, the relative benefit of DMTs is consistent across these groups. As part of the subgroup analysis considering the interaction with DMTs, no significant interactions were observed between DMTs and sex assigned at birth (p=0.573) or SMN2 copy number (p=0.672). These results support the generalisability of therapeutic benefit irrespective of these individual characteristics. Overall, these findings, even if limited to a relatively short follow-up period, provide initial evidence that DMTs in type III individuals have an impact on LOA. In approximately a third of the individuals who lost ambulation, this occurred in individuals who already had limited mobility at the time when DMT was started, suggesting that early treatment—particularly in type IIIA—may prevent or delay LOA. The use of time-dependent survival analysis provided further information on the influence of other variables. Individual risk factors such as sex, SMN2 copy number and age at symptom onset influence the overall progression and risk of LOA. However, these factors do not appear to significantly modify the therapeutic response as this can be observed in the whole group of treated individuals irrespective of these variables. These results highlight the sustained benefit of treatment across a broad spectrum of individuals and reinforce the role of early and proactive management to preserve motor function and long-term mobility in type III. chunks.content: Introduction Over the past 2 or 3 decades, there has been a steady increase in the number of children receiving long-term home respiratory support (HRS) [ ]. This trend can be attributed to several factors, including advancements in medical technologies and novel therapies, such as treatments for spinal muscle atrophy (SMA). These advances have improved survival rates and heightened awareness of sleep-related breathing disorders (SRBDs), leading to more widespread screening in at-risk populations, such as patients with neuromuscular disorders (NMDs) or trisomy 21, and the availability of home-based ventilation systems [ , ]. Additionally, ventilators designed specifically for children and infants, as well as tailored interfaces like masks for non-invasive ventilation (NIV), have become more accessible. The evolution of ethical perspectives has further supported this shift. Consequently, many patients who would not have survived to adulthood only a few decades ago now transition to adult care, necessitating that specialists develop expertise in the management of these complex conditions. When caring for children requiring long-term respiratory support, several general considerations should be kept in mind. Firstly, there is an exponential increase in the number of children being considered for such support. Secondly, the complexity of cases with HRS is steadily increasing. Thirdly, each patient requires an individualized approach, as is applied across a highly heterogeneous spectrum of diseases. Fourthly, multiple coexisting factors, such as obesity, bronchial aspiration leading to secondary pneumopathy, muscle weakness, central causes, or upper airway collapse (e.g., in cerebral palsy), must be considered, as they can influence the indication for respiratory support and can contribute to chronic respiratory failure. Close follow-up is essential for children on long-term respiratory support to tailor the care plan to their growth and disease progression and to assess therapy adherence, a task often challenging in paediatrics. Neurocognitive impairment is common among this patient population and can significantly impact therapy feasibility and implementation. Many children who require long-term respiratory support present with comorbidities affecting multiple organs, often within the context of complex chronic disorders. This necessitates a multidisciplinary approach, with care ideally coordinated through a case manager, or preferably, an integrated care model. For families caring for a child with special needs, this situation can impose a significant financial burden and negatively affect the health of other family members, leading to issues such as sleep disturbances or psychological stress [ , ]. This article provides comprehensive paediatric recommendations for Switzerland, including indications and guidance on establishing an optimal care team. It outlines the necessary materials and equipment and their practical applications, and further addresses therapeutic education, follow-up procedures, ethical considerations, and the transition to adult care [ ]. Methodology All members of the “Special Interest Group in paediatric Home Mechanical Ventilation” of the Swiss Society of Paediatric Pulmonology (SSPP) were invited to participate in a task force aiming at establishing recommendations on paediatric long-term HRS in Switzerland. These recommendations are based on an extensive review of the medical literature over the past 5 years through PubMed, of other national guidelines, and of the specifics of paediatric care for long-term HRS in Switzerland. Following the 2022 European Respiratory Society (ERS) statement on paediatric long-term non-invasive respiratory support [ ] that included publications up until September 2019, we performed a MEDLINE search for the period running from October 2019 until May 2023. Search terms were those cited in the ERS publication (“Continuous Positive Airway Pressure” “CPAP,” “NCPAP,” “bi-level ventilation,” “BPAP,” “BiPAP,” “airway pressure release ventilation,” “APRV,” “noninvasive ventilation,” “NIV,” “NPPV,” “NIPPV,” “NIAV,” or Invasive Ventilation “IV” with a child and adolescent search filter). Inclusion criteria were articles published in English for humans aged <18 years. Exclusion criteria were articles not published in English, as well as those concerning neonatology or intensive care settings, acute or emergency conditions, acute infections, COVID-19, or case reports. We also took into account recent national guidelines from German- and French-speaking countries that we are familiar with. Two independent reviewers (R.C. and I.R-M.) screened a total of 592 articles, of which 260 met the inclusion criteria. The final text was discussed in depth among the members of the SSPP’s Special Interest Group in paediatric Home Mechanical Ventilation to reach a consensus. This document focuses on HRS that covers also mechanical ventilation delivered in long-term care institutions, providing indications, modalities, and follow-up recommendations for patients on HRS (e.g., continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP], NIV, IMV, etc.). This document does not cover NIV in the acute setting (emergency ward, intensive care unit [ICU], acute-care hospital wards) or the adult population. General Considerations Indication Long-term mechanical ventilation is feasible at any age, including in newborns and infants [ , ]. In younger patients, invasive ventilation (IV) is often preferred to NIV due to factors such as underlying pathology, physiologically longer sleeping hours, and the unavailability of appropriately sized masks for NIV. The medical conditions necessitating long-term mechanical ventilation are diverse and often overlap in individual patients ( ). Depending on the underlying pathology and the progression of the disease, it is sometimes possible to transition from IV to NIV (e.g., in cases of congenital central hypoventilation syndrome) [ ] or, conversely, from NIV to IV (e.g., in NMDs) [ ]. Initiation Criteria for Respiratory Support Initiation criterion for respiratory support in children is a subject that is still sparsely discussed in the literature in an integrated approach. Standardizing decisions on measured values is only a piece of the puzzle and depends on the underlying disease and the individual clinical and social conditions. General Remarks Medical indications: The decision to initiate ventilation is primarily guided by the medical needs of the child. Feasibility for the child and family: An individualized approach with every decision tailored to the unique circumstances of the patient and family, ensuring that medical, practical, and ethical concerns are balanced [ ]. Multifactorial assessment: The decision to introduce ventilation should not rely on a single parameter but rather on a comprehensive evaluation. Major factors to consider include the following: – Severity and duration of symptoms: Assess the severity and length of symptoms, with specific thresholds guiding initiation. – The presence of clinical indicators should inform the decision, such as increased work of breathing while awake, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, or symptoms of SRBD (e.g., snoring, choking, or gasping during sleep) [ , ]. – Abnormal gas exchange: Identify significant deviations in gas exchange values. Oxygen levels: Similarly, oxygen thresholds lack consensus and should be contextualized within clinical findings. Capnia levels: While there is no consensus on acceptable levels, ERS guidelines provide general reference points. Nocturnal hypoventilation is defined by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) as pCO 2 >50 mm Hg for >25% of total sleep time. Other sources propose a more restrictive definition, which should also be considered in clinical decision-making [ ]. For example, thresholds for NMDs may be stricter [ ]. – The assessment of sleep integrity and the presence of sleep apnoea as contributing factors are important based on polysomnographic or polygraphic findings using paediatric index values. – Lung function measurements could also be considered (e.g., a decline in vital capacity). – Special consideration for specific illnesses, such as SMA or NMDs, must be made by medical teams in charge of the patient. HRS for Obstructive Sleep Apnoea HRS for Infants and Young Children (1–23 Months Old) with Obstructive Sleep Apnoea . Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) severity should be determined based on polysomnographic findings. Where polysomnography (PSG) is unavailable, polygraphy (PG), or at least oxi-capnometry, can be considered as alternative diagnostic tools. An obstructive apnoea-hypopnea index (AHI) ≥1/h is considered abnormal at this age. Whether HRS is indicated depends on numerous other factors, and expected benefits must be carefully weighed against treatment burden and expected outcome [ ]. These additional factors influencing the decision include the presence of comorbidities (e.g., craniofacial malformations); risk factors, including developmental delays, growth issues, or a history of a brief resolved unexplained event; apparent upper airway obstruction during wakefulness; or the occurrence of recurrent infections. HRS for Children with Persistent OSA (2–18 Years Old) . According to the ERS Guidelines, HRS therapy should be considered when OSA persists after a stepwise approach. Persistent OSA (6 to 9 months) is defined based on a sleep study, with a recommendation for HRS as follows: (1) AHI >5/h – HRS is recommended irrespective of the presence of morbidity; (2) AHI 1–5/h – treatment may still be beneficial, especially in the presence of cardiovascular morbidity, central nervous system morbidity, enuresis, somatic growth delay or growth failure, decreased quality of life, or risk factors for persistent SRBD [ ]. If diagnostic tools such as PSG or PG are unavailable for SRBD patients, treatment may be considered based on positive oxi-capnometry findings, validated SRBD questionnaires, or evidence of morbidity. For these patients, HRS can also be a first-line treatment in cases where other interventions (e.g., adenotonsillectomy) are not indicated or feasible. The American Thoracic Society (ATS) recommendations for persistent OSA are stricter, defining persistent OSA as AHI >1/h. They propose to consider HRS therapy for children with

central nervous system morbidity, enuresis, somatic growth delay or growth failure, decreased quality of life, or risk factors for persistent SRBD [ ]. If diagnostic tools such as PSG or PG are unavailable for SRBD patients, treatment may be considered based on positive oxi-capnometry findings, validated SRBD questionnaires, or evidence of morbidity. For these patients, HRS can also be a first-line treatment in cases where other interventions (e.g., adenotonsillectomy) are not indicated or feasible. The American Thoracic Society (ATS) recommendations for persistent OSA are stricter, defining persistent OSA as AHI >1/h. They propose to consider HRS therapy for children with persistent OSA and who are not candidates for surgery. While HRS or surgery was historically reserved for cases of AHI ≥5/h, this treatment option is now increasingly considered for children with milder symptoms but persistent morbidity. A more precise definition and additional criteria relating to persistent OSA remain to be better defined in order to improve future patient care [ ]. Invasive Ventilation The decision to initiate IV should be made by the physician, considering all relevant clinical factors, including patient history, the severity of respiratory failure, and the expected evolution. If a patient requires NIV for more than 16 h per day, this may indicate the need for IV [ ]. Some patients may even stay for 24 h under NIV, especially those capable to use mouthpiece ventilation. In neonates and young infants, invasive long-term ventilation is often required in conditions such as severe chronic respiratory failure, including bronchopulmonary dysplasia, childhood interstitial lung diseases, congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, or NMDs. Patients may also require IV if they fail to wean from a ventilator in the ICU as following surgery or in the case of spinal cord or brainstem injuries/lesion and if weaning to NIV is not feasible. For patients with progressive diseases who require ventilatory support, the potential need for IV should be evaluated early. The possibility of transitioning to IV should be addressed openly with the patient and family, respecting the patient’s preferences in decision-making. These criteria emphasize early assessment, continuous monitoring, and involving the patient and their family in discussions around the need for IV ( ). SSPP Recommendations: Considerations before Initiating Respiratory Support in Children Initiating respiratory support in children, especially those with complex or chronic conditions, is a multifaceted decision that requires careful consideration and a multidisciplinary approach. The SIG group recommends taking into account the following points in the decision-making process: 1. Indications for long-term ventilation: Long-term HRS may be justified when the child has been unable to wean from IV or CPAP/NIV after being treated in the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU). Weaning failure may indicate that the child’s respiratory system requires ongoing support, either due to chronic disease or insufficient recovery. 2. Ventilation strategy in newborns: For newborns, both term and preterm, a gradual transition from permissive ventilation to targeted eucapnic ventilation will facilitate the optimal ventilatory support in the evolving respiratory system of the child. 3. Screening for SRBD: Children with conditions that increase the risk of SRBD – such as craniofacial malformations or NMDs – should undergo PSG or PG prior to elective surgery. If SRBD is confirmed, HRS should be considered to minimize perioperative risks, including failed extubating or difficulties during recovery from anaesthesia. This proactive measure may help prevent complications and reduces the risk of intraoperative complications. In addition, prior difficult airway experiences, i.e., failed extubation, or prolonged recovery period should be inquired and addressed prior to surgery. 4. Hospital and intensive care competence in paediatric respiratory support: The hospital in which respiratory support is initiated should be equipped with a PICU or within a hospital network with established links to a specialized paediatric centre, as initiation carries risks, including complications that may require advanced monitoring and immediate medical intervention. For complex or high-risk patients, the hospital team should be well versed in paediatric respiratory care and have access to resources for managing potential complications. Caveats for Respiratory Support Technical progress in interfaces and machines should always be checked against individual patient needs, taking into account the patient’s and family’s quality of life. Anatomical barriers for ventilatory support include mid-face anomalies for NIV or a short neck for tracheostomy. Prolonged use of CPAP or NIV beyond 12–16 h per day might indicate that more intensive ventilatory support (IV) is needed. Uncontrolled or severe gastroesophageal reflux can increase the risk of aspiration, which may require invasive management. Inadequate swallowing function or bulbar involvement that leads to aspiration risk. If the patient cannot adequately protect his/her airway, such as in cases of neurological impairment, non-invasive options may not be sufficient and IV with a cuffed tracheal canula would be needed. Recent upper airway or craniofacial surgery in these areas can compromise the effectiveness or safety of CPAP or NIV. If optimal CPAP or NIV cannot correct issues such as OSA or hypoventilation/hypercapnia, if children remain dyspnoeic, or if a proper interface (mask or nasal cannula) cannot be adequately fitted to the patient, IV may be considered. If the patient cannot tolerate the mask or device, it may not be a sustainable option. Lack of cooperation from patient and/or family with a non-compliance or unwillingness to use CPAP or NIV effectively. Clinical Considerations to Not Initiate IV In some situations, initiating IV may not be appropriate. These include the following: If the prognosis is poor and further medical interventions, including IV, are unlikely to provide meaningful benefit, it may not be appropriate to proceed with IV. Certain anatomical or medical conditions, such as a short neck, may preclude the possibility of performing a tracheostomy, making IV less feasible or safe. IV should not be initiated if it goes against the expressed wishes of the patient or their family. If the patient or parents are unfit to decide, we could proceed as the patient’s best care stands first. Shared decision-making is crucial in these circumstances [ ]. There may be ethical concerns surrounding the use of IV, particularly if it contradicts principles such as autonomy, the patient’s quality of life, or the potential for suffering [ , ]. Futile prognosis. These factors emphasize a patient-centred, ethical approach to decision-making, where both clinical guidelines and individual patient preferences are considered. SSPP Recommendations: Minimal Requirements for Initiation of Ventilation When considering outpatient initiation on ventilation, certain key factors need to be met to ensure treatment safety and effectiveness. These include the following: Stability of the patient: – The patient should be in a stable clinical condition, with no acute exacerbations. – Adequate management of any underlying medical condition should be set up to prevent complications during outpatient treatment. Age: – Children who are older than kindergarten or primary school age are considered suitable candidates for outpatient initiation. Younger children may need more intensive monitoring and care, which may require inpatient initiation. – However, age alone is not a strict determinant, and this criterion should be adjusted based on the specific needs of the child and family. Mode of monitoring: – Regular follow-up and monitoring are essential to track the patient’s response to treatment and adjust care as needed. – A monitoring plan must be established, and the appropriate mode of monitoring (e.g., pulse oximetry, capnography, etc.) should be discussed and agreed upon by the healthcare team. Parental comfort: – Parents and caregivers must feel comfortable and confident in managing the ventilation equipment, including using and maintaining the devices, and responding to any emergencies or complications. – This may include training on equipment use, troubleshooting, and emergency procedures. Healthcare team expertise to begin ventilation: – The healthcare team should have expertise in managing patients considered for outpatient ventilation, including knowledge of the specific type of ventilation used, and monitoring strategies for outpatient management. A multidisciplinary approach involving respiratory therapists, nurses, and physicians may be necessary to ensure comprehensive care. These minimal requirements aim to ensure that the outpatient initiation of ventilation is safe, effective, and sustainable for the healthcare team, the patient, and their family. Optimal Care Team A multidisciplinary team approach is essential for delivering optimal care when considering ventilation, to ensure that children receive the appropriate respiratory support. Each team member’s expertise should combine experience in both paediatric and neonatal intensive care, to ensure that children across all age ranges can be managed effectively and safely. Collaboration among paediatric medical doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, and other specialists is key to providing holistic care tailored to each child’s individual needs. When transitioning to home care, a compromise must be found between ensuring the best possible safety for the child and meeting the realistic requirements of the family and caregivers. Aspects to consider include the child’s medical needs and the family’s capacity to provide the necessary care. The requirements for care team support at home depend on several factors. Mode of HRS (e.g., NIV vs. tracheostomy). Degree of ventilator dependence (whether the child can breathe spontaneously for certain periods). Cognitive and neuromuscular capacity of the patient (degree of independence of the child has, and level of assistance needed). Degree of caregiver comfort, which can vary widely among families. The ATS recommends that a trained caregiver should always be present in the home when a child requires chronic IV. At least two family member caregivers should be trained to provide care to ensure constant coverage. Professional healthcare providers are not required to always be present at home but must be available for guidance and emergency situations. It is essential that 7/7 technical support is available for children on invasive HRS. This should include a hospital backup, ensuring a hospital team is available for emergencies or guidance, including trained professionals who can assist with routine outpatient care and emergency situations, a paediatrician able to provide ongoing health care and coordinate with specialists when necessary, and social workers to support the family with emotional, logistical, and financial challenges that may arise from the complex care needs [ ]. Material support to ensure ventilator replacement including other devices as suctioning device needs to be available 24 h/day 7/7. The content of training for parents and caregivers is crucial but often not clearly defined. Ideally, standardized training on routine care and emergency measures should be provided to improve the confidence and competence of caregivers. The education programmes should focus on (1) routine care (e.g., managing ventilator equipment, airway clearance, monitoring respiratory status) and (2) recognition and management of emergencies (e.g., dealing with ventilator malfunctions, respiratory distress, or aspiration events). Material/Equipment Ventilators and HRS Devices There are two distinct types of respiratory devices, each serving a unique purpose: life support devices and non-life support devices ( ). The performance of ventilators may not always be optimal for paediatric patients, particularly in terms of trigger sensitivity. Therefore, they must be carefully adjusted to suit each patient’s specific needs. Additionally, these devices are typically approved by manufacturers with specific minimum weight requirements. It is currently recommended that a single-limb circuit with intentional leaks is safely utilized in out-of-hospital settings, including for IV [ ]. Choice of Ventilator or HRS Device The selection of a ventilator or HRS device is determined by the patient’s medical needs and individual characteristics. The lack of standardized nomenclature for modes and settings results in significant variability between manufacturers and devices. Due to weight restrictions of various devices, life support devices are often utilized for very young children, even if they are not entirely dependent on them. The constant pressure (CPAP)p is the first-line treatment for paediatric SRBD. More advanced modes, such as auto-CPAP, are reserved for selected patients. High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) may be considered an alternative treatment for patients intolerant to CPAP. Tracheotomized patients should always be equipped with a device approved for IV. A backup life support device will become necessary when dependence on respiratory support exceeds 16 h per day [ ]. Ventilator Settings Setting ventilatory parameters must consider each patient’s unique physiological and respiratory characteristics. For a purely obstructive respiratory pattern, such as persistent OSA, titration with CPAP alone may suffice [ – ]. In contrast, patients with a mixed central and obstructive pattern, as seen in neuromuscular conditions, require a tailored approach. This includes determining the optimal mean airway pressure for oxygenation, achieving the best minute ventilation (MV), and incorporating a backup respiratory rate (BURR) to effectively regulate PCO 2 levels. The AASM recommends using titration in ventilation initiation with a PSG to determine optimal inspiratory positive airway pressure (IPAP) and expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) levels [ ]. However, adequate titration may also be achieved without a full PSG or with a PG only [ , ]. In addition, other objective assessment tools exist to help titrate settings and to achieve clinical efficacy [ , , ]. The choice of ventilation is also a matter of debate. Indeed, even if initiating CPAP in children with OSA is considered safe, it does not show superiority over bi-level pressure ventilation in terms of comfort and adherence [ ]. In contrast, HFNC may serve as a more tolerable alternative treatment for paediatric OSA, though current evidence supporting its efficacy remains limited [ ]. The different ventilatory modes available are dependent on treatment goals and the patient’s needs, including bi-level, pressure control, volume control, trigger types, and variations in inspiratory time. The starting pressures could be EPAP: 4 centimetres of water (cm H 2 O), or IPAP: 8 cm H 2 O [ – ]. To address alveolar hypoventilation, a tidal volume of 6–10 mL·kg −1 is recommended. Sometimes, higher pressure levels may be necessary for children with advanced disease or requiring IV [ ]. Comparing performance, adherence, and complication risks among mask interfaces in paediatric patients is challenging as shown in . Most available data are derived from adult studies. Close monitoring and a proactive approach are crucial to minimize complications and optimize the use of HRS in home settings. Interfaces can be categorized into five types: nasal mask, oronasal mask, full-face mask, nasal prongs, and mouthpiece [ ]. 1. Nasal masks/nasal prongs are well tolerated, pose minimal risk of aspiration, and allow for effective communication with the patient. Nasal masks are safer because they allow unimpaired spontaneous breathing in case of equipment failure. An optimal fit of the nasal mask with no leak despite minimal tension of the straps improves comfort and compliance and reduces the risk of mid-face hypoplasia. 2. Oronasal or full-face masks help reduce mouth leaks but may limit communication capabilities. They are associated with a higher risk of aspiration, potential skin injuries, and lower tolerance [ – ]. 3. Mouthpieces are suitable only for awake and cooperative patients who can create a seal around the mouthpiece with their lips. These devices enable communication and pose no risk of aspiration or skin injury. The choice of interface depends on several factors, including the provider’s experience, the availability of interfaces that suit the patient’s morphology, the patient’s tolerance, and the ability to meet initial respiratory support goals [ , ]. The selection of the correct size for a tracheal cannula is also critical. Indeed, to enable vocalization or speech, the cannula must provide enough space around the trachea for adequate airflow flux. For this reason, the type of tracheal cannula should be tailored to the patient’s needs, and testing distinct types may help identify the most suitable option. High-Flow Nasal Cannula HFNC has shown promise in various settings; however, its use in home paediatric ventilation should always be guided by professional clinical judgement and tailored to individual patient needs. HFNC is a safe and effective method for improving oxygenation and reducing the work of breathing through the delivery of continuous humidified air/oxygen, and it also tends to be better tolerated and accepted by children. The enhanced comfort provided by this respiratory support device often leads to greater satisfaction among patients and their parents. However, HFNC has no internal battery and needs sector electricity. Additionally, its cost-effectiveness in reducing hospital admissions is currently under evaluation. Current HFNC indications are as follows: Obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS) [ , ]. Tracheomalacia [ ]. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia [ ]. Severe forms of childhood interstitial lung disease and end-stage cystic fibrosis [ ]. Intolerance to CPAP in OSAS [ ]. In case of intolerance to the NIV or CPAP mask, the RAM cannula or the Optiflow™ interface can be considered [ , ]. Heating of the Ventilator Tubing Heating of the tubing helps reduce condensation [ ], leading to turbulent airflow, which may participate in patient-ventilator asynchrony (e.g., auto-triggering) or result in the spillage of condensate into the patient’s mask/airway. Smaller children are particularly vulnerable to these issues. To avoid heating trouble, it is proposed to heat the tubing to enhance treatment adherence. The need for heating depends on the initial pathology, the patient’s age, and the type of ventilation used. Adjustments should be tailored to individual patient needs. The heating temperature varies between 34° for NIV and 37° for IV. To avoid mould developing, the water present in the humidifier needs to be changed every day. Heated humidification and HME are the two most used methods of artificial humidification in ventilated patients. However, HME should be carefully evaluated in patients with limited respiratory reserve due to the resistance it may induce. SSPP Recommendations: Devices and Setting of Devices Each centre should define a limited set of devices for each type of respiratory support (life support, life sustaining, CPAP). This allows a better knowledge of the material by all team taking care of these patients. The selection of a device should be based on the child’s characteristics, medical needs, and the preferences of the paediatric care team. Off-label use of some devices may need to be considered for selected patients (e.g., life support device in infants with need of CPAP, toddlers’ CPAP device although approved at >30 kg). Bi-level positive pressure support ventilation in spontaneous/timed mode (S/T) is commonly used in clinical practice. Starting inspiratory and expiratory pressures are set at 8 cm H 2 O and 4 cm H 2 O, respectively, with a final IPAP of 10–14 cm H 2 O and EPAP of 4–6 cm H 2 O. Pressures, however, must be tailored to patient’s needs, and pressures outside the recommended range might be required both for EPAP and for IPAP for selected patients, especially for children with NMDs who often are more efficiently ventilated with lower EPAP. Adverse Effects and Their Management Various adverse effects associated with respiratory support devices have been documented in the literature, affecting approximately one-third of the paediatric population, despite medical staff’s awareness of these risks. Monitoring and addressing these complications are essential to ensure good adherence to therapy by both patients and their families. The most frequent side effects are as follows: 1. Skin injuries that must be systematically monitored at each consultation [ – ]. 2. Air leaks around the mask, leading to xerophthalmia or conjunctival irritation, typically due to poor fitting (shape, size) or improper positioning, must be consistently monitored during consultations [ , , ]. 3. Nasal symptoms, such as dryness, nasal congestion, or bleeding, that affect 5–38% of patients and can be improved with humidification and/or heated circuits [ , ]. 4. Mid-face anomalies, which may develop with long-term NIV/CPAP, especially if initiated early in life, and depend on the type of mask and the patient’s genetic susceptibility. A maxillofacial and orthodontic evaluation is recommended if needed. A mid-face hypoplasia occurs in 3–37% of patients, with a higher incidence in younger children. Changing the interface can modify pressure points on the patient’s face [ , ]. 5. Risk of broncho-aspiration, particularly with oronasal masks in patients with NMD. Other interfaces should be considered for these individuals [ ]. 6. Abdominal distention and discomfort. 7. Pneumothorax, although its occurrence is infrequent [ , ]. A well-structured follow-up enhances the ability to adapt HRS to the patient’s evolving needs, including pressure adjustments or device modifications, as well as adjustments in response to changes in the family’s daily life over the years. The frequency of follow-up after the initiation of HRS depends on multiple factors, such as the patient’s age, underlying diagnosis, ventilation mode, available support services, and monitoring capabilities. Typically, the first visit should be scheduled 1–3 months after starting, followed by regular visits every 3–6 months [ , ]. For patients who are clinically stable and less dependent on respiratory support, annual visits (every 12 months) may be appropriate [ ]. After each intervention, such as changes in ventilator settings or surgical procedures, a sleep study should be conducted to verify effectiveness of the HRS settings [ ]. Software Download, Oximetry, Capnometry, PG, PSG In general, younger, and/or clinically unstable children require shorter intervals between hospital visits and data collection to facilitate timely treatment adjustments. Most HRS devices have a built-in software that allows the download of respiratory parameters. These data may help improve HRS settings during follow-up visits, but they must be used with caution in children, as AHI scoring by the device may be over- or underestimated [ – ]. Analysis of built-in software data is therefore complementary and useful but cannot replace sleep studies. Follow-ups on HRS should include at least overnight monitoring of gas exchange by oximetry (oxygen saturation [SpO 2 ] measurement) and capnometry (transcutaneous estimation of PaCO 2 measurement) [ ]. Oximetry alone is insufficient for the evaluation of respiratory support as SpO 2 is not necessarily indicative of effective ventilation [ ]. These measurements may be performed at home [ ]. In Switzerland, several providers, such as the Lung Leagues and various device companies, deliver a home service to collect measurements and transmit data to physicians. PSG or PG can provide essential information to improve control of SRBD [ , ]. In several international guidelines, regular PSG/PG is recommended for the evaluation of child on HRS [ , , ]. Adherence and Compliance Data Poor adherence to treatment is a major challenge in long-term HRS for children [ , – ]. The aim is consistent use of CPAP/NIV throughout the entire sleep period. Although no validated definition of optimal adherence exists for children, it should be maximized through individually tailored strategies [ – ]. For children who rely on NIV as life support, optimizing adherence is critical and requires continuous reassessment. Adherence should be evaluated at every visit using objective data from the HRS device’s built-in software, as children and caregivers often overestimate actual use [ ]. Telemedicine and Telemonitoring Telemedicine represents one of the most promising advancements in the management of NIV. Recent innovations aim to identify potential issues more quickly, enabling timely interventions before the next scheduled in-person visit. Telemonitoring with remote data analysis from HRS devices’ built-in software and home-recorded sleep studies is feasible. This approach offers a convenient way for both patients and physicians to verify and adjust HRS settings, as well as manage respiratory exacerbations [ – ]. Videoconferencing has also been shown to be beneficial in the management of children, fostering high levels of family confidence in clinical decisions and offering value to clinicians in their decision-making process [ , ]. However, it remains unclear whether these approaches are cost-effective, or if they improve outcomes or adherence to treatment in children [ , ]. SSPP Recommendations: HRS Follow-Up The first visit after initiation of HRS should be scheduled at 1–3 months, followed by regular visits every 3–12 months, which should include monitoring as described below. Monitoring HRS efficiency should at least include analysis of device data and measurement of gas exchange (oximetry and capnometry). An adequate ventilation (pCO 2 <6.5Pa or significant decrease from the initial value) and oxygenation, a normal work of breathing while awake, and an absence of symptoms of SRBD are essential to evaluate the efficiency of the HRS adjustment. If possible, use also regular PSG/PG. Adherence to HRS should be assessed at every visit. Lack of adherence should trigger investigation on patient-ventilator asynchrony and mask leaks, and other reasons of discomfort, closer follow-ups, and additional home support should be offered. It is important to recognize when the entire system or family is struggling with adherence and provide extra help and support. While telemonitoring and telemedicine show promise, they should complement, not replace, regular face-to-face visits. Telemonitoring needs to be well documented and define clear responsibility for follow-up and adjustment of settings. Weaning Unlike invasive mechanical ventilation, weaning, or failure thereof, has not been clearly defined for patients on non-invasive respiratory support. This lack of standardization is critically important, as maintaining unnecessary ventilatory support can be intrusive, while premature discontinuation may lead to increased morbidity and prolonged ventilation duration. Unfortunately, there are only a few studies in the literature that provide detailed weaning criteria [ , ]. It is important to highlight that not all children on HRS can be weaned; this depends largely on the underlying disorder. For children with severe lung disease, weaning from respiratory support could be due to natural improvement over time and enhanced respiratory muscle strength, with weaning potentially occurring through spontaneous recovery, physiological growth, or sometimes following specific interventions (e.g., orthodontic treatment, surgical procedure), nutritional support, or weight loss, particularly in cases of OSAS [ ]. Weaning is first initiated during daytime while the child is awake, with the duration off the ventilator gradually increased. Weaning from nocturnal use occurs only once the child can remain off the ventilator while awake. Regular clinical assessments should include measuring SpO 2 and PCO 2 to monitor tolerance. Signs of weaning failure include rising transcutaneous estimation of PaCO 2 , recurrent pneumonias, growth failure (due to increased caloric expenditure from the work of breathing), with reduced energy available for activities which enhance quality of life. In addition, parents should be taught to observe the child for signs of respiratory distress and report any concerns to healthcare providers. A washout period may be necessary during weaning, during which HRS is temporarily discontinued prior to performing a sleep study. Non-Invasive HRS Failure Several factors can contribute to the failure to initiate or maintain non-invasive respiratory support. A thorough understanding of the psychosocial context of the child and family, as well as the treatment goals, is essential, as these aspects can significantly impact the success of ventilation and must be carefully evaluated by the medical team. There is a lack of precise definition for non-invasive HRS failure in the paediatric population. Distinct factors such as mask discomfort, asynchrony, and major leaks likely have a negative impact on adherence. The cognitive status, psychosocial context, domestic environment, and the cooperation of both the child and their family are thought to play a determining role in success or failure. Based on factors identified as contributing to non-invasive HRS failure, targeted interventions can be proposed to address the specific challenges [ ]. SSPP Recommendations: HRS Weaning The following recommendations are proposed regarding HRS weaning or failure: Initiate daytime weaning while the child is awake, progressively increasing the extent of time without the respiratory support. Only proceed with nighttime weaning once the child can tolerate extended periods off the ventilator during the day. Monitor for rising PCO 2 levels, development of pneumonia, and signs of growth failure, which may result from increased caloric expenditure due to the effort of breathing and can lead to less energy available for activities that enhance quality of life. Mask discomfort, asynchrony, and major air leaks have a negative impact on NIV adherence, while cognitive status, psychosocial context, domestic environment, and the cooperation of both the child and their family are suspected to play a determinant role in NIV success or failure. All these aspects need to be considered to allow successful use of HRS. Traveling Travel has become a common part of life for most ventilated children today. Enabling families to maintain a sense of normality should be a shared goal for each patient and their medical team. Supporting this helps both the patient and their family to experience a more typical and fulfilling lifestyle. Traveling with HRS is possible but requires careful anticipation and planning. For patients with nocturnal HRS, daytime travel may be preferred to align with their respiratory needs. Key considerations include the following: Journey conditions (e.g., accessibility to electricity during travel). Conditions at the destination (e.g., proximity to a hospital capable of handling respiratory exacerbations). The flight duration should also be considered. Patients will need to check whether they need to apply for airline (operator) approval for carrying and using the respiratory device, including the battery. Patients should carry the device as hand luggage and have a hospital letter explaining the need for HRS. In serious cases like patients needing oxygen or with severe conditions, a hypoxic challenge test may be considered before travel to assess altitude tolerance. For children ventilated invasively with a cuffed canula, the cuff pressure must be adjusted when flying at high altitudes due to the risk of cuff expansion leading to tracheal injury. Mechanical Insufflation/Exsufflation for Neuromuscular Patients Devices for mechanical insufflation/exsufflation (MIE) assist children with impaired coughing ability by applying positive airway pressure (insufflation) followed by a rapid shift to negative pressure (exsufflation) to simulate a natural cough [ , ]. The indications for MIE are the presence of secretions that the patient cannot effectively cough up on his own. In adults, cough peak flow (CPF) values <270 L/min are a relative indication, while values <160 L/min are an absolute indication. Such thresholds described in the literature do not apply to children, particularly younger ones [ ]. In children, reference values and thresholds of CPF are age and, from the onset of puberty, sex dependent [ ]. CPF values <50% of median reference values correspond to a CPF <270 L/min in adults. MIE is most effective in children who can cooperate, typically from 3 to 5 years of age. Early use is encouraged for all patients with airway clearance difficulties to prevent and treat pulmonary complications [ – ]. The interfaces for MIE devices can be used with a facial mask, mouthpiece, or tracheostomy cannula. Initiation typically begins with lower insufflation and exsufflation pressures, gradually increasing as tolerated. Reported pressure ranges are between 10 and 50 cm H 2 O for insufflation and between −10 and −60 cm H 2 O for exsufflation. All settings are adjusted with growth, using longer times and higher pressures as children grow. Asymmetric pressures (e.g., higher insufflation or lower exsufflation pressures) can address issues like abdominal distention, reflux, or emesis. There are no clear guidelines regarding optimal MIE settings in children. Existing guidelines are derived from algorithms and can only serve as a guide for initiation [ , ]. Families can use MIE devices at home after receiving training by physiotherapists, nurses, or device-specific staff. Combining MIE with manually assisted cough techniques improves outcomes [ , , ]. Adherence can be a challenge, and barriers to regular use must be identified and addressed [ , ]. While pneumothorax is a theoretical risk, no direct cases have been reported in children. SSPP Recommendations: MIE for Neuromuscular Patients The following recommendations are proposed regarding the use of MIE: Early use in infants: MIE may be beneficial even in infants, potentially from the first year of life, depending on the disease and the child’s level of cooperation. When to initiate: MIE should be introduced to reduce the risk of recurrent respiratory infections and in children with a stable respiratory condition. NMD patients requiring ventilatory support should, with few exceptions, be started on MIE; it may serve also for lung-volume recruitment. Pressure and adaptation: MIE pressures must be tailored to the child’s age, clinical needs, and tolerance. Regular reassessment of settings and techniques is essential to ensure ongoing effectiveness and safety. Implementation: Initial MIE sessions should be conducted by a physiotherapist, ideally in a hospital ambulatory setting. Transition to home use requires proper training and monitoring by experienced professionals. Caregivers should also receive training to handle respiratory tract infections and aspiration events. Creating a context in which the patient is able to take decisions freely may improve adherence care and facilitate transparent discussions among the patient, physicians, and family [ ].

Ethics HRS in paediatrics represents a highly specific context of care, frequently raising ethical challenges due to the lack of scientific data and literature to guide decision-making, particularly in cases where patients refuse HRS. The extreme heterogeneity of situations (including pathology, age, prognosis, and family context) together with the need for tripartite decision-making involving the medical team, the patient, and the parents further complicates both medical and ethical considerations. Creating a context in which the patient is able to take decisions freely may improve adherence care and facilitate transparent discussions among the patient, physicians, and family [ ]. The patient should have the final decision provided they have the capacity to do so. The decision-making process should promote a factual risk-benefit analysis and consider not only the child’s physical benefit, but also impact on quality of life and consequences on others [ ]. This is a dynamic and evolving process, and the decision whether to apply HRS should be re-evaluated regularly. The medical team should ensure that patients and family are aware that no decision is definitive. A decision to not apply HRS should be accompanied by alternative support and palliative care [ ]. Finally, the decision must be documented in the medical file. SSPP Recommendations: HRS and Ethics The following recommendations are proposed regarding ethical considerations: 1. Promote discussions based on a factual description of treatment risks and benefits. 2. Consider the principles of beneficence and non-maleficence in each decision, in close discussion with the patient and their family. The decision to apply or not HRS results from a joint decision-making process that should include all the medical teams taking care of the patient, the patient, and his/her family. 3. Ensure equity between patients by avoiding subjective projections, balancing the financial burden between society and the patient, and considering the broader consequences of each decision for both the patient and their family. The medical team should anticipate the child’s loss of communication or comprehension skills [ ]. 4. Consider cultural background, individual believes, and the family environment at each stage of discussion and decision. 5. Reassess all decisions regularly and depending on the patient’s evolution. HRS in Palliative Care and Patients with Neurological Impairments HRS has been proposed in several palliative situations, including severe neuro-disability, but very few data are available. Consequently, clear indications and prescription criteria are limited by the lack of scientific arguments for and against HRS. The efficacy of HRS has been reported in specific contexts and considered in specific palliative situations, including severe neuro-disability. It is important to highlight that it can increase survival, reduce time spent in hospital, and improve children’s quality of life. HRS can contribute to the improvement of sleep, sleep apnoea, and quality of life in children with severe neuro-disability. Each decision must be documented in the medical file, including, as with any ethical discussion, the objective and expected benefits of care. The care plan should define the modalities best suited to the objectives: type of HRS, location and method of implementation, trial duration, success criteria, failure criteria. The decisions should include anticipated directives in case of acute decompensation. Ultimately, the efficacy of HRS in palliative situations is defined by improvement of comfort, reductions in hospital stay duration, and alleviation of dyspnoea. Transition The transition period to adult care represents a critical time for young adults requiring long-term HRS, often marked by a conflict between their desire for independence and the increasing healthcare needs associated with the progression of their underlying disease. To date, most paediatric pulmonary services responsible for these patients lack standardized transition programmes, which may leave them without structured guidance during this crucial phase. However, there is growing evidence that implementing a standardized transition process can significantly improve outcomes, as patients demonstrate better compliance with treatment and enhanced self-management skills. A well-designed transition program should consider the unique medical and psychosocial needs of everyone, offering personalized plans that emphasize education and training to foster self-management. Collaboration between paediatric and adult care teams is essential to ensure continuity of care, while also addressing the emotional and psychological challenges that often accompany this transition. Standardizing the process not only eases the burden on patients and families but also promotes independence and long-term adherence to care, underscoring the importance of investing in structured transition pathways for this vulnerable population [ ]. The transition is a maturation process and must start early to provide the time needed for preparation. It involves the patient, parents, therapists, and doctors [ ]. During this period, a care coordinator is crucial, especially for patients with cognitive impairments who may not be fully capable of self-care. Rare diseases or conditions with unexpected outcomes (e.g., SMA type 1) further highlight the importance of a structured transition process. Finally, adult care teams may lack experience in rare respiratory conditions, emphasizing the need for a well-organized transition plan. A coordinated effort between paediatric and adult care is essential to bridge knowledge gaps and ensure continuity. A structured transition also helps prevent interruptions in care that could compromise the patient’s future well-being. Conclusion The number of patients requiring long-term mechanical ventilation is rapidly increasing. Clinicians must adapt their practices not only by regularly updating available technologies but also by evolving their approaches to the care of patients transitioning into adulthood. Drawing from limited paediatric literature and expert consensus, we propose follow-up strategies designed to support the development of standardized care. Ultimately, multicentre studies and the establishment of national and international guidelines will be essential to improve and harmonize follow-up and weaning practices for children on home mechanical respiratory support. chunks.content: Introduction The 2010 care considerations for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) , advocated a multidisciplinary approach to the management of this severe, progressive neuromuscular disease. This three-part update was necessitated by a number of themes that characterise contemporary DMD care: the increasing complexity of subspecialty care and the need for a multidisciplinary clinical team; the use of more sensitive diagnostic techniques and earlier therapeutic interventions; the expectation of prolonged survival, prompting the need for care guidance across the lifespan; and the recognition that the natural history of DMD has been altered by the long-term use of glucocorticoids. The new care considerations have also been shaped by the expectation that emerging genetic and molecular therapies will substantially change the nature of DMD management in the near future. In 2014, the DMD Care Considerations Working Group steering committee, comprising experts from a wide range of disciplines, identified 11 topics to be included in this update. Part 2 contains the latest care considerations for respiratory, cardiac, bone health and osteoporosis, and orthopaedic and surgical management. Large-scale, randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are rare in this field, so guidance was developed using a method that queries a group of experts on the appropriateness and necessity of specific assessments and interventions, using clinical scenarios. This methodology was designed to produce an essential toolkit for DMD care; only assessments and interventions that have been deemed both appropriate and necessary are recommended. A complete description of the methods is provided in part 1 and the . in part 1 of this Review provides a brief overview of assessments and interventions across all topics, organised by stage of disease. It is intended to serve as a pocket guide to overall disease management. Respiratory management Respiratory complications are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in people with DMD. Complications include respiratory muscle fatigue, mucus plugging, atelectasis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure. If left untreated, patients are at risk of severe dyspnoea, lengthy hospital admissions due to atelectasis or pneumonia, and death due to respiratory arrest or respiratory-induced cardiac arrhythmias. - An anticipatory approach to management includes monitoring of respiratory muscle function and the timely use of lung volume recruitment, assisted coughing, nocturnally assisted ventilation, and subsequent daytime ventilation. These core therapies can decrease respiratory complications, improve quality of life, and prolong survival. , - Patients should typically be using most or all of these core therapies by the age of 18–21 years, before their transition from paediatric to adult respiratory care providers. Implementation of respiratory care considerations and guidelines , , - requires a multidisciplinary team— including physicians, respiratory therapists (or physical therapists in some health-care systems), and home caregivers—to perform pulmonary function testing and sleep studies and to initiate and manage lung volume recruitment, manual and mechanically assisted coughing, , non-invasive ventilation, and invasive ventilation via tracheostomy. Decisions for optimum respiratory management need to be made with awareness of the patient’s other body systems, especially the cardiac system. , In this update, we endorse higher pulmonary function thresholds (ie, milder levels of respiratory impairment) for initiation of assisted coughing and assisted ventilation than were recommended in the 2010 care considerations. The new criteria are intended to result in more anticipatory use of these interventions, with the possibility that therapy will be initiated in slightly younger patients. Ambulatory stage shows respiratory diagnostic tests and therapies for individuals with DMD, by stage of disease. Spirometry should be initiated when the patient is 5–6 years of age. Serial monitoring of pulmonary function is critical for respiratory management. Typically, forced vital capacity (FVC) rises with growth, until an individual becomes non-ambulatory. FVC reaches a peak, followed by a plateau, and then deteriorates over time. - Deteriorating FVC can occur in the absence of dyspnoea and remain unrecognised unless pulmonary function is measured regularly. In a large cohort study in boys who had not been treated with corticosteroids, the age at loss of ambulation was predictive of the age at which peak FVC was realised, the absolute peak FVC, and the rate of subsequent decline. For example, earlier loss of ambulation was associated with an earlier and lower peak FVC as well as a more rapid decline in FVC than was later loss of ambulation. However, because the rate of change in FVC over time can vary greatly among individuals, serial measurement of FVC is necessary to characterise each individual’s respiratory phenotype or trajectory.
